title: Query readability and CTE pipelines
objective: Refactor nested, repetitive queries into a pipeline of named CTE steps (filter → enrich → aggregate → rank/compare → present) that returns exactly the same, well-defined result.
context: You inherited a folder of 'working' queries written as five-level-deep subqueries. Nobody dares touch them. Your lead asks you to rewrite each one as a readable CTE pipeline before the Snowflake migration — same output, but reviewable.

exercises.title: High-value customers, untangled
exercises.question:
Refactor this query (it lists high-value customers):
SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, x.rev FROM customers c JOIN (SELECT customer_id, SUM(q*p) rev FROM (SELECT o.customer_id, oi.quantity q, oi.unit_price p FROM orders o, order_items oi WHERE o.order_id = oi.order_id AND o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')) GROUP BY customer_id) x ON x.customer_id = c.customer_id WHERE x.rev >= 1000
exercises.prompt: Write it as a CTE pipeline returning customer_id, name, gross_revenue (rounded to 2 decimals) for existing customers whose gross revenue is at least 1000. Valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); gross revenue = SUM(quantity * unit_price) over those orders' order_items lines (never products.list_price).
hints: Innermost first: the subquery with the status filter becomes CTE #1 (valid_lines).
CTE #2 aggregates per customer; the final SELECT joins customers and applies the >= 1000 filter.

WITH valid_lines AS (...), customer_revenue AS (SELECT customer_id, SUM(line_revenue) AS gross_revenue FROM valid_lines GROUP BY customer_id) SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, ROUND(cr.gross_revenue,2) AS gross_revenue FROM customer_revenue cr JOIN customers c ... WHERE cr.gross_revenue >= 1000;
exercises.why: The old version hid the business rule inside the deepest subquery and used comma joins. The pipeline makes the rule visible on line 4.

recall.q: In which order should CTEs appear?
recall.a: In data-flow order: each CTE only references CTEs defined above it.

exercises.snowflake: Identical in Snowflake; you could also write `GROUP BY ALL` in customer_revenue.

exercises.title: Monthly revenue with month-over-month change
exercises.question: Refactor: SELECT m, r, r - (SELECT SUM(oi2.quantity*oi2.unit_price) FROM orders o2 JOIN order_items oi2 ON oi2.order_id=o2.order_id WHERE o2.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned') AND strftime('%Y-%m', o2.order_date) = strftime('%Y-%m', date(m || '-01', '-1 month'))) FROM (SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', o.order_date) m, SUM(oi.quantity*oi.unit_price) r FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id=o.order_id WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned') GROUP BY 1) WHERE m LIKE '2025%'
exercises.prompt: Return order_month ('YYYY-MM'), gross_revenue, prev_month_revenue (the previous calendar month's gross revenue; for 2025-01 that is 2024-12) and mom_change (gross_revenue − prev_month_revenue), all rounded to 2 decimals, for each 2025 month that has valid orders. Every month from 2024-12 to 2025-12 has valid orders, so LAG over the monthly rows gives the previous calendar month. Valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); gross revenue = SUM(quantity * unit_price) over those orders' order_items lines (never products.list_price).
hints: Replace the correlated subquery with LAG() over a monthly CTE.
Filter to 2025 AFTER computing LAG, otherwise January loses its December 2024 comparison.

WITH valid_lines AS (...), monthly AS (... GROUP BY order_month), with_prev AS (SELECT ..., LAG(gross_revenue) OVER (ORDER BY order_month) AS prev_month_revenue FROM monthly) SELECT ... FROM with_prev WHERE order_month LIKE '2025%';
exercises.why: Correlated subqueries that recompute an aggregate per row are slow and hard to read; a window over a small monthly CTE is both faster and clearer.

recall.q: Why must the 2025 filter come after the LAG step?
recall.a: Because WHERE runs before window functions in the same SELECT; filtering first removes 2024-12, so January's LAG would be NULL.

exercises.snowflake: Same pipeline with DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date); the final filter can be a QUALIFY on the LAG step.

exercises.title: Net revenue by category
exercises.question:
Refactor this three-level query that finance can't read:
SELECT cat, g, IFNULL(rf,0), g-IFNULL(rf,0) FROM (SELECT IFNULL(p.category,'Uncategorized') cat, SUM(oi.quantity*oi.unit_price) g, SUM((SELECT SUM(r.refund_amount) FROM returns r WHERE r.order_item_id=oi.order_item_id)) rf FROM order_items oi JOIN products p ON p.product_id=oi.product_id WHERE oi.order_id IN (SELECT order_id FROM orders WHERE order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')) GROUP BY 1)
exercises.prompt: Return category (NULL as 'Uncategorized'), gross_revenue, refunds (sum of returns.refund_amount on those lines, 0 if none) and net_revenue (gross_revenue − refunds), all rounded to 2 decimals. Valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); gross revenue = SUM(quantity * unit_price) over those orders' order_items lines (never products.list_price). Net revenue = gross − refunds.
hints: Steps: valid lines → refunds per line (pre-aggregated) → enrich with category → aggregate.
LEFT JOIN the refunds CTE so lines without returns keep refund 0.

WITH valid_lines AS (...), line_refunds AS (SELECT order_item_id, SUM(refund_amount) AS refund FROM returns GROUP BY order_item_id), enriched AS (... LEFT JOIN line_refunds ...) SELECT category, ROUND(SUM(line_revenue),2) AS gross_revenue, ...
exercises.why: Pre-aggregating refunds to the line grain in its own CTE makes it obvious that the join can't fan out.

recall.q: Why pre-aggregate returns before joining them to lines?
recall.a: To guarantee at most one row per line, so line revenue is never duplicated even if a line had several returns.

exercises.snowflake: Identical; NVL(p.category, 'Uncategorized') and ZEROIFNULL(lr.refund) are the Snowflake spellings.

exercises.title: Cohorts and repeat customers
exercises.question: Refactor: SELECT f, COUNT(*), SUM(CASE WHEN n > 1 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) FROM (SELECT customer_id, (SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', MIN(order_date)) FROM orders o2 WHERE o2.customer_id=o.customer_id AND o2.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')) f, COUNT(*) n FROM orders o WHERE order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned') AND customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM customers) GROUP BY customer_id) GROUP BY f
exercises.prompt: Return cohort_month (the 'YYYY-MM' of each customer's first valid order), customers (number of customers in the cohort) and repeat_customers (how many of them have 2 or more valid orders). Only existing customers (present in customers); valid = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned').
hints: The correlated MIN subquery and the COUNT(*) both describe one customer — compute them together in one GROUP BY.
valid_orders CTE → per_customer CTE (cohort_month + order count) → group by cohort.

per_customer AS (SELECT customer_id, strftime('%Y-%m', MIN(order_date)) AS cohort_month, COUNT(*) AS valid_orders FROM valid_orders GROUP BY customer_id) SELECT cohort_month, COUNT(*) AS customers, SUM(CASE WHEN valid_orders >= 2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS repeat_customers ...
exercises.why: Two passes over the same table collapse into one aggregate once each step has a name.

recall.q: What is the grain of the per_customer CTE?

exercises.snowflake: per_customer: SELECT customer_id, DATE_TRUNC('month', MIN(order_date)) AS cohort_month, COUNT(*) AS valid_orders ... final: COUNT_IF(valid_orders >= 2) AS repeat_customers.

exercises.title: Best-selling product per category
exercises.question: Refactor: SELECT cat, pn, u FROM (SELECT IFNULL(p.category,'Uncategorized') cat, p.product_name pn, SUM(oi.quantity) u FROM order_items oi JOIN products p ON p.product_id=oi.product_id JOIN orders o ON o.order_id=oi.order_id WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned') GROUP BY 1,2) t WHERE u = (SELECT MAX(u2) FROM (SELECT IFNULL(p2.category,'Uncategorized') c2, SUM(oi2.quantity) u2 FROM order_items oi2 JOIN products p2 ON p2.product_id=oi2.product_id JOIN orders o2 ON o2.order_id=oi2.order_id WHERE o2.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned') GROUP BY 1, p2.product_id) WHERE c2 = t.cat)
exercises.prompt: Return category (NULL as 'Uncategorized'), product_name and units_sold (sum of quantity on valid orders, order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')) for the top-selling product of each category (there are no ties at the top).
hints: The same aggregation is written twice in the old query — write it once as a CTE.
Rank inside each category with ROW_NUMBER() and keep rn = 1.

WITH product_units AS (...GROUP BY category, product_id, product_name), ranked AS (SELECT ..., ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY units_sold DESC, product_id) AS rn FROM product_units) SELECT ... WHERE rn = 1;
exercises.why: Duplicated subqueries drift apart over time (someone fixes one copy). One CTE = one definition.

recall.q: What replaces 'WHERE x = (SELECT MAX(x) ... correlated)' in a pipeline?
recall.a: A window function (ROW_NUMBER/RANK) in a CTE, filtered with WHERE rn = 1 (QUALIFY in Snowflake).

exercises.snowflake: ... FROM product_units QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY units_sold DESC, product_id) = 1;

exercises.title: Year-over-year customer growth
exercises.question: Refactor: SELECT c.customer_id, c.name, (SELECT SUM(oi.quantity*oi.unit_price) FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id=o.order_id WHERE o.customer_id=c.customer_id AND o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned') AND o.order_date LIKE '2024%') a, (SELECT SUM(oi.quantity*oi.unit_price) FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id=o.order_id WHERE o.customer_id=c.customer_id AND o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned') AND o.order_date LIKE '2025%') b FROM customers c WHERE b > a
exercises.prompt: Return customer_id, name, revenue_2024, revenue_2025 and growth (revenue_2025 − revenue_2024), all money rounded to 2 decimals, ordered by growth descending then customer_id — only for customers whose 2025 gross revenue is strictly greater than their 2024 gross revenue AND who had revenue in both years. Valid orders = order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned'); gross revenue = SUM(quantity * unit_price) over those orders' order_items lines (never products.list_price).
hints: Two near-identical correlated subqueries → one CTE with conditional aggregation (SUM(CASE WHEN year ...)).
A customer with no 2024 revenue has revenue_2024 NULL, and NULL comparisons are not true — so they drop out, as required.

yearly AS (SELECT customer_id, SUM(CASE WHEN order_year='2024' THEN line_revenue END) AS revenue_2024, ... GROUP BY customer_id) SELECT ... FROM yearly y JOIN customers c ... WHERE y.revenue_2025 > y.revenue_2024 ORDER BY growth DESC, c.customer_id;
exercises.why: Conditional aggregation in one pass replaces N correlated subqueries — the classic readability *and* performance win in pipeline refactors.

recall.q: Why use SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN x END) without ELSE 0 here?
recall.a: So a year with no revenue stays NULL and fails the > comparison — 'had revenue in both years' comes for free.

exercises.snowflake: yearly: SUM(IFF(YEAR(order_date) = 2024, line_revenue, NULL)) AS revenue_2024, ... (or PIVOT).

worked_example.question: Rewrite `SELECT customer_id, total FROM (SELECT customer_id, SUM(v) AS total FROM (SELECT o.customer_id, oi.quantity*oi.unit_price AS v FROM orders o JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id=o.order_id WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')) GROUP BY customer_id) WHERE total > 1500` as a pipeline.
worked_example.sql:
WITH valid_lines AS (
    SELECT o.customer_id, oi.quantity * oi.unit_price AS line_revenue
    FROM orders AS o
    JOIN order_items AS oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
    WHERE o.order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
), customer_revenue AS (
    SELECT customer_id, ROUND(SUM(line_revenue), 2) AS gross_revenue
    FROM valid_lines
    GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT customer_id, gross_revenue
FROM customer_revenue
WHERE gross_revenue > 1500;
worked_example.explanation: Same logic, but each step has a name a reviewer can check on its own (you can even `SELECT * FROM valid_lines` while debugging). The innermost subquery became the first CTE.

recipe:
**Recipe: from nested soup to a CTE pipeline in 5 moves**

1. **Read inside-out** and write down what each subquery *means* in one phrase ("valid orders", "line revenue").
2. **Name each step** as a CTE, in the order data flows: `valid_orders → order_lines → customer_revenue → ranked`.
3. **One responsibility per CTE:** filter, *or* join, *or* aggregate. Define business rules (valid statuses,
   revenue) exactly once, in the first CTE that needs them.
4. **Finish with a thin final SELECT** that only picks, renames and orders columns.
5. **Prove equivalence:** same row count and totals as the old query (`EXCEPT` both ways should return nothing).

```sql
WITH valid_orders AS (      -- 1. filter
    SELECT order_id, customer_id, order_date FROM orders
    WHERE order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
), lines AS (               -- 2. enrich
    SELECT vo.customer_id, oi.quantity * oi.unit_price AS line_revenue
    FROM valid_orders vo JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = vo.order_id
), per_customer AS (        -- 3. aggregate
    SELECT customer_id, SUM(line_revenue) AS gross_revenue FROM lines GROUP BY customer_id
)
SELECT * FROM per_customer;  -- 4. present
```
snowflake_notes:
CTEs work identically in Snowflake, and they're the backbone of dbt models (each model is usually a chain of
`import → logical → final` CTEs).

```sql
WITH valid_orders AS (
    SELECT * FROM orders WHERE order_status IN ('completed','shipped','returned')
),
monthly AS (
    SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) AS order_month, SUM(quantity * unit_price) AS gross_revenue
    FROM valid_orders JOIN order_items USING (order_id)
    GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT order_month, gross_revenue,
       gross_revenue - LAG(gross_revenue) OVER (ORDER BY order_month) AS mom_change
FROM monthly
QUALIFY order_month >= '2025-01-01'           -- QUALIFY can filter after LAG has seen 2024 rows
ORDER BY order_month;
```

- Snowflake's optimizer inlines CTEs (or materialises ones referenced several times), so readability usually costs nothing.
- Snowflake allows **lateral column aliases**: `SELECT a + b AS total, total * 0.1 AS tax` — handy, but not portable.
- `SELECT * EXCLUDE (col)` and `GROUP BY ALL` keep final SELECTs short.
- For very long pipelines prefer **views / dbt models** for reusable steps, and temporary tables
  (`CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE ... AS`) only when an intermediate result is reused by many queries.
common_mistakes: Copy-pasting the business rule (valid statuses) into several CTEs instead of defining it once at the top.
Filtering too early in a pipeline that later needs the filtered rows (e.g. LAG across a year boundary).
CTEs named cte1, cte2, t, x — the name should say what the rows ARE.
Mixing grains in one CTE (some columns per line, some per order) — keep one grain per step.
Not proving the refactor: compare row counts and totals against the old query before replacing it.
recall: What does each CTE in a good pipeline do?
Exactly one job (filter, join, aggregate or rank) at a clear grain.
How do you prove a refactor returns the same rows?
(old EXCEPT new) and (new EXCEPT old) both return zero rows; also compare counts/totals.
Can a CTE reference a CTE defined below it?
No (except a recursive CTE referencing itself); define them in data-flow order.
review_next: Lesson 46 asks whether a readable query is also an efficient one: sargable predicates, filtering early, pre-aggregation — and how Snowflake prunes micro-partitions.
